rationale: CSS backdrop-filter was a scalar blur radius end to end. The canvas exposed only save_backdrop_filter(x, y, w, h, blur_radius), so saturate(), brightness(), invert(), grayscale(), sepia(), contrast(), hue-rotate() and any composition of them were parsed and discarded, and a design that desaturates what is behind an element rendered it at full saturation. Adds Canvas::save_backdrop_filter_chain taking the same FilterChainEntry list the foreground filter chain already used, with a default that sums blur entries and drops the rest so every existing backend keeps exactly the behaviour it had; a new CanvasCapability::backdrop_filter_chain lets a caller tell the two apart rather than infer faithfulness. The Skia override reuses the element-layer chain builder, now extracted as compose_css_filter_chain, so the two layers cannot drift into disagreeing about what saturate(0.15) means. The one non-obvious part is the crop: SkImageFilters::ColorFilter reports unbounded output, so saveLayer treats its bounds as a hint and grows the layer to the device clip, and the filtered result then composites over everything already painted -- the whole panel floods with one colour. The composed chain is therefore wrapped in SkImageFilters::Crop; cropping only the blur entry, which is what the blur-only path did because a blur was the only unbounded thing it could produce, is not sufficient. This is the same unbounded-output trap already documented one function away for the crt shader effect. Measured against Chrome on a probe design that uses these filters, area-weighted failing fraction improves 0.3220 to 0.0035 with ink coverage 0.9986 to 0.9994; no design in the current corpus declares a non-blur backdrop-filter, so the corpus numbers are unchanged. drop-shadow() in a backdrop list and url(#filter) remain unsupported and are named as such in the ledger. Pulp-only: the gap and the fix both originate here, with no counterpart framework change to backport. Bundling four weights of Jost changed nothing, because the bundled-typeface cache keys one face per family name and every weight of a family reports the same family name — CoreText answers "Jost" for Jost-Regular through Jost-Bold alike. The first blob declared won the key and the other three were dropped at registration, so the binary carried six faces and the cache held three. match_bundled_typeface then compared the surviving 400 face against the request and missed every non-400 weight, sending measurement to a platform substitute; the SkParagraph bridge, reading the same cache, registered one face under "Jost" and SkParagraph faux-emboldened it. Traced before changing anything: at 400/500/600/700 the resolver answered Jost-Regular/Helvetica/Helvetica/Helvetica and the paragraph path answered Jost-Regular four times, painting 461/461/606/606 ink px for one string — two synthesis steps, not four weights. A family now holds every face that reports its name, and both the bundled cache and the plugin registry select through one shared three-pass style matcher (exact, then nearest same-slant within one CSS weight step, then variable-axis eligibility), so a family that ships a single Regular still declines a Bold and lets the cascade reach a system face. After: four distinct faces on all three surfaces and 438/481/538/580 ink px at 15px, 3523/4226/4707/5117 at 48px. Measured against Chrome on the design corpus, forge moves 0.1678 to 0.1691 and delay 0.0967 to 0.0968 area-weighted failing at unchanged 1.0000/0.9998 ink coverage — the metric gets marginally worse because Chrome laid every Jost run out on Regular's advances and added synthetic ink for the heavy ones, which is what the broken path was accidentally reproducing; the correct static SemiBold and Bold are 7-11% wider by their own hmtx. Jost 400, where the face was already right, holds at 0.0% ink-width error against Chrome before and after, which is what says the measurement chain is sound and the residual is a static-versus-variable face difference rather than a regression. Pulp-only: the defect and the fix both originate here. Re-deriving a line break inside a box that the break itself determined is not reliable at any metric quality. An auto-width label's box was sized BY its own text, so it has no slack, and any positive epsilon in a measured advance pushes the last word onto a second line; Pulp measures a captured string about 0.65% wider than the browser's own line box for reasons not yet explained. Label therefore gains an optional CACHE of a browser's line breaking — rects plus UTF-16 offsets — used verbatim while the conditions that produced it still hold, and discarded for a normal reflow the moment they do not. The node stays one semantic paragraph, so accessibility, selection, translation and edit addressing are unaffected and reflow remains available; this is the same measure-once-reflow-forever shape PreparedText already implements, with the expensive measurement arriving from outside. Invalidation is deliberately conservative: the resolved face identity (a PostScript name, not the requested family, since one family covers several instances that break differently), the container width the text was broken at, and the text content itself; anything unknown counts as a mismatch, because a wrongly reused cache reintroduces the defect while a wrongly discarded one costs only a reflow. FontResolver gains resolved_face_identity so a caller outside the canvas can ask which instance a family stack resolves to without reaching for Skia types. Measured against Chrome on the design corpus, delay improves 0.1020 to 0.0965 area-weighted failing at unchanged 100% ink coverage. Pulp-only: the defect and the fix both originate here, with no counterpart framework change to backport. Text resolved one face for measurement and a different one for paint, and resolved every weight as Regular. Two independent defects with the same signature. First: fill_text resolves an SkFont through FontResolver — bundled faces included — then uses it only for a coverage check and paints through SkParagraph, which re-resolves from a FontCollection. text_font_context.cpp bridged the bundled faces into that collection only when the platform had no font database of its own, so on macOS every family resolved through CoreText and an imported panel painted every run in one system fallback while measuring each correctly; four Labels with four different families measured 253/253/262/317 and painted at an identical 258.5px ink width. The bridge is now unconditional, which is what the deferring comment described as the right fix. Second: TextShaper::prepare took no weight, measure_segment hard-coded SkFontStyle::Normal, and the segment cache was keyed on family and size alone, so a Bold run and its Regular twin shared one set of advances and a variable font could not be measured at the requested weight at all — instancing the wght axis lives in FontResolver and nothing on that path called it. Weight now travels through prepare into both cache keys, and measure_segment's hand-rolled cascade is replaced by the shared resolver, which also ends a quieter divergence where segment widths and line metrics could resolve different faces for one family stack. Label gains effective_font_weight() because an imported design sets weight on the view via set_inheritable_font_weight, leaving Label::font_weight() at its 400 default. Jost is bundled alongside Inter and JetBrains Mono: imported designs ask for it, no host ships it, and the substitute is about 10% wider per glyph. Measured against Chrome on the design corpus, delay improves 0.1020 to 0.0973 area-weighted failing at unchanged 100% ink coverage; bold agrees with Chrome's own weight cost to 0.009px. Pulp-only: the defects and the fixes both originate here, with no counterpart framework change to backport. CSS letter-spacing follows every character rather than sitting between them, and SkParagraph — which paints the run — adds it that way too, but Label::intrinsic_width reserved one step per GAP. Layout therefore sized every letter-spaced label one step short of what got drawn, so the glyphs ran past the box Yoga sized for them and a row of such labels measured narrower than it paints. Established against Chrome rather than from the spec: a census walks a capture directory, shapes each line's exact substring through the same TextShaper the layout path measures with, and compares the advance to Chrome's own per-line textBox width. Over 410 lines from four captured designs the per-character convention lands on -0.02% median error across the 89 letter-spaced lines and the per-gap convention on -2.86%; on a single-character run — where per-gap reserves nothing at all however wide the spacing — the gap convention is off by up to 21%. The census is kept as a hidden test so the comparison can be re-run against any capture, and it corrects for an ancestor transform scale, because Chrome reports a text box in the transformed space while font-size stays the untransformed computed value and a panel that fits itself to a viewport with scale(.9) otherwise reads as every run inside it being 11% too wide. Two neighbouring facts the same measurement settles, neither addressed here: text inside such a scaled wrapper renders 11% too wide in the native design lowering (+10.99% median ink width over 13 runs, against +0.00% over the 11 outside it), and TextShaper::prepare carries no letter-spacing at all, so line BREAKING ignores it — latent, since no wrapping run in the corpus is letter-spaced. Pulp-only: the defect and the fix both originate here. Whole-tree lowering deliberately does not carry `transform`, because the box a node is placed by is already the transformed rectangle. That is true of the box and false of everything inside it: Chrome scales the glyphs along with the box, so a pre-scaled box filled with the untransformed `font-size` drew every run 1/scale too wide. On forge, 25 of 39 text runs sit under one `transform: matrix(0.9,0,0,0.9,0,0)` wrapper and the headline 'What do you want to build?' rendered 11.10% long, ending at x=1904 against Chrome's x=1800. Lowering now folds the accumulated ancestor scale into font-size, letter-spacing and line-height. Ancestor chains multiply rather than taking the nearest wrapper's factor. A chain that does not reduce to one positive uniform scale — two axes, a flip, a rotation, a matrix3d — is REFUSED and recorded per node as `type_scale_refused` plus a `native_nodes_type_scale_refused` count, because type carries a single scalar and a plausible wrong number is harder to find later than a recorded refusal. Measured: the headline goes to +0.00% and ends at x=1800, Chrome's own pixel; forge's rendered ink width across every measurable run moves from median +7.04% p95 +11.63% to median +0.00% p95 +1.16%, and for the 16 runs under the wrapper from +10.85% to +0.00%; area-weighted failing 0.1691 to 0.1635 and the text feature 0.4384 to 0.3634 at unchanged 1.0000 coverage. Designs with no transform are untouched, asserted by byte equality rather than by argument: delay and spectr render 0 changed pixels and hold at 0.0944 and 0.1245. A new capture fixture renders one string twice at an identical computed style where the only difference is a scale(0.5) wrapper — Chrome reports 143.188px and 286.375px — so a lowering that ignored the transform cannot pass by arithmetic over the computed style alone.
